place.en: Black Pine Ridge · under the cliff

setup.zh: 谷口的藤墙为她让开了路；她咳出一口银色的血，化成小狐狸伏在你肩上发抖。你顺着自己的记号爬上石缝；崖顶上，爹在喊你的名字。
setup.en: The wall of vines parts for her; she coughs silver blood and becomes a small fox trembling on your shoulder. You follow your own marks up the rock; at the top, Father is calling your name.

recap.zh: 你顺着记号爬上了崖，爹一把抓住了你——他在崖边趴着喊了你一夜；天亮时，阿禾的爹老周顺着你的记号寻了进来。银月咳着银色的血，伏在你肩上，只有你看得见。
recap.en: You climbed back up by your marks and Father caught your hand — he had lain at the edge calling you all night; at dawn Ahe's father, Old Zhou, followed your marks in. Yinyue, coughing silver blood, lay on your shoulder, seen by you alone.

zh: 肩上一团银，一直在发抖。
en: The wall of vines opens a way.
A curl of silver on your shoulder, trembling.
From the clifftop, a hand reaches down.

story.zh:
沈小满这一辈子，欠过许多人的账。欠阿禾的鸡蛋，欠吴婆婆的鹿腿，欠他娘的一只碗，欠马家的——不对，马家的不算，照他自己的说法，马家的是马家欠他的。这些账，后来他一笔一笔都还了，有的还了本，有的连利息也还了，还有的，利息比本钱还大。

只有一笔，他到老也不知道该怎么还。那是一个谢字。说来好笑，一个字，不值一文钱，张嘴就有，可他欠了她这一个字，从蒙山的谷底一直欠到了后来的许多许多年。这一回书，说的便是这个字，是怎么欠下的。

那山谷的出口，是沈小满找着的。

小满便想起他爹的话来：先看风，后看鹿。这谷里没有鹿，只好看风。他从头上拔下一根头发——这回学乖了，离银月远远的——捏着举在半空。那头发起先软塌塌地垂着，过了一会儿，微微地往西一飘，又一飘，飘得很是坚决。风是从东边来的。这谷四面是崖，崖上垂着藤，照理说，风该在谷里打转，转得昏头昏脑，哪里有这般一个劲儿往一处吹的道理？除非东边有一个口子，外头的风从那口子里灌将进来。

他顺着风往东走，银月跟在后头。走不多远，谷底收窄了，两边崖壁越挤越近，挤到后来，只剩一道一人来宽的石缝，缝口上密密层层挂满了藤，藤条比他胳膊还粗，一根缠着一根，一层压着一层，便是一只兔子也休想钻得过去。可风是从藤缝里钻进来的，凉飕飕的，带着一股松针的味道。那是黑松岭的味道。小满凑近了闻，心里一酸，险些没掉下泪来——这辈子头一回觉得，黑松岭的味道这么好闻。

他回头道：「出口在这儿。」

银月早已站在他身后了，懒洋洋地抬了抬下巴，道：「本王正要说。」

小满瞧着那面藤墙，心里盘算：柴刀昨儿滚下崖的时候丢了，拿手扯，扯到明年开春也扯不开；拿牙咬，牙口倒是不错，只是咬开这一面墙，只怕这一口牙也要跟家里那几只碗一般，个个缺口了。他正算着，银月已越过他走上前去，对着那面藤墙，淡淡地说了两个字：「让开。」

只见那藤墙簌簌一抖。跟着，便像一群给主人喝住了的狗，一根一根，缩头缩脑地缩了回去，缩得又快又乖，有几根缩得慢了，还给旁边的藤挤了一下。不过眨眼之间，藤墙上已让出一条刚够一个人走的路来，路上连一片叶子都没留下。

小满张大了嘴，回头看她。便在这时，他瞧见她身子晃了一晃，伸手捂住了嘴，咳了一声。这一声咳得极轻，她的指缝里却漏将出来几滴东西，落在草上，亮晶晶的，是银色的血。

小满抢上一步要去扶，手还没伸到，她已不见了。只觉肩膀上一沉，一只巴掌大的小银狐已蹲在了那里，尾巴绕过他的脖子，凉凉的，软软的。它嘴也没动，声音却直接落进了他的耳朵里：「看什么。本王跌得只剩金丹，修为十成去了九成，化形撑不了多久。……走你的路。」

小满僵着脖子，一动也不敢动，生怕一动，它便从肩膀上滑下去，问道：「别人看得见你吗？」

「本王只肯让你看见。别人看你，就是一个脖子上缠了条灰不溜秋旧狗皮的傻孩子。」

小满想了一想，说道：「……那我得先谢谢你。」

「谢什么？」

「这是我这辈子，穿过最贵的衣裳。」

它没有说话，可趴在他肩上的那团毛，一直在抖，也不知是笑的，还是冷的，还是疼的。小满没有问。他家的规矩，疼了不说，也没人问，这规矩他昨儿夜里刚跟它说过，今儿自己倒先守上了。
story.en:
In his life Shen Xiaoman ran up a great many debts. He owed Ahe eggs, owed Granny Wu a leg of venison, owed his mother a bowl, owed the Mas — no, the Mas didn't count; by his own reckoning, it was the Mas who owed him. Every one of those debts he paid back in the end, stroke by stroke; some he paid the principal, some the interest too, and some the interest came to more than the principal.

Only one he never knew, even when he was old, how to repay. It was the word *thanks*. Funny, when you think about it: one word, not worth a copper, there for the saying the moment you open your mouth — yet he owed her that one word from the bottom of the valley on Mount Meng for many, many years after. This part of the story tells how that debt was run up.

It was Shen Xiaoman who found the way out of the valley.

Xiaoman remembered his father's saying: first read the wind, then the deer. There was no deer in this valley, so he'd read the wind. He plucked a hair from his head — having learned his lesson, well away from Yinyue this time — and held it up. At first it hung limp; after a while it drifted west, and again, quite decidedly. The wind was coming from the east. With cliffs on every side and vines hanging from them, the wind ought to be going round and round in circles, dizzy as a drunk — why would it keep blowing one way like that? Unless there was a gap to the east, and the wind outside was pouring in through it.

He followed the wind east, Yinyue behind him. Before long the valley floor narrowed, the cliff walls pressing closer and closer until only a crack a man wide was left, its mouth hung thick with vines, each thicker than his arm, one tangled round the next, layer on layer — not even a hare could have squeezed through. Yet the wind was coming through the vines, cool, carrying the smell of pine needles. The smell of Black Pine Ridge. Xiaoman leaned in and breathed it, and his heart ached so that he nearly cried — for the first time in his life, Black Pine Ridge smelled good.

He turned round. "The way out's here."

Yinyue was already standing behind him. She lifted her chin lazily. "This king was just about to say so."

Xiaoman eyed the wall of vines and did his sums: his chopper had been lost tumbling down the cliff yesterday; tear at it by hand and he'd still be tearing next spring; bite through it — his teeth were good enough, only after biting through a wall like this they'd be as chipped as the bowls at home. While he was still reckoning, Yinyue stepped past him, faced the wall of vines, and said two words, flatly: "Make way."

The wall of vines gave a rustling shudder. Then, like a pack of dogs scolded by their master, the vines drew back one by one, heads ducked, quick and meek; a few that were slow even got jostled by their neighbours. In the blink of an eye a path just wide enough for one person had opened in the wall, not a single leaf left on it.

Xiaoman's mouth fell open and he turned to her. Just then he saw her sway, raise a hand to her mouth, and cough. It was a very soft cough, but something leaked between her fingers and fell on the grass, glittering: silver blood.

Xiaoman sprang forward to steady her, but before his hand reached her she was gone. There was a weight on his shoulder: a palm-sized silver fox crouched there, its tail curled round his neck, cool and soft. Its mouth didn't move, but its voice dropped straight into his ear: "What are you looking at. This king has fallen as far as a golden core, nine parts in ten of my cultivation gone; a human shape doesn't hold for long. …Walk your road."

Xiaoman held his neck stiff, not daring to move for fear it would slide off. "Can other people see you?"

"This king lets only you see. To anyone else you're a silly boy with a scruffy old grey dog pelt round his neck."

Xiaoman thought a moment and said, "…Then I'd better thank you first."

"For what?"

"This is the most expensive thing I've ever worn."

It said nothing, but the fur lying on his shoulder kept shivering — whether from laughing, or cold, or hurting, who knew. Xiaoman didn't ask. His family's rule: when it hurts you don't say, and nobody asks. He'd only told it that rule last night, and here he was keeping it first.

exits.means: climbs up, takes father's hand, goes back to him

what.zh: 天亮时顺着你刻的记号寻进黑松岭，扛着门板来找你。
what.en: At dawn he followed the marks you cut into Black Pine Ridge, carrying a door-plank to bring you home.

story.zh:
他把脸侧过去一点，对着肩上那团毛，清了清嗓子。有些话，他想，是该趁着这时候说的。昨儿夜里跟它说了一整夜的话，说娘，说爹的膝盖，说阿禾的鸡蛋，说那只碗，天南海北，说了个遍，却偏偏漏了这一句。它帮他开了藤墙，咳出了血；它昨儿夜里差一点没了气——这些，都得跟它说清楚。他便郑重其事地道：「银月。」

「嗯。」

「昨儿夜里……不对，今儿早上……也不对。」他想了一想，决定不去管是什么时候了，「反正，我想跟你说——」

「你爹在上面喊你。」

小满一愣。

「喊了一夜了，」它的声音很低，「嗓子哑了，你听不出来。本王听得出。……先应他。」

小满竖起耳朵往上听。风从崖顶上刮下来，呜呜的，风里头，果然夹着一个声音，哑得几乎听不出是人声，一遍一遍，喊的是他的名字。那声音喊一声，歇一歇，再喊一声，喊得极慢，倒像每一声都要从嗓子眼里一点一点地抠出来。

他张开嘴想应，一张嘴，才发觉自己的嗓子也哑了——昨儿夜里跟一只狐狸说了一整夜的话，说哑的。他憋足了一口气，扯着嗓子喊了一声：「爹——！」这一声喊出来，又破又尖，跟一只给踩了尾巴的鸭子差不多。上头那个喊声，登时便断了。

跟着上头便乱了起来。先是一个粗嗓门叫道：「——这儿！坡上的泥，塌了一大块！底下有人！」却是阿禾她爹老周。跟着是七嘴八舌的人声，脚步声，有人在喊「绳子！绳子！」有人在喊「慢着，别都挤在边上，这坡还在往下掉土」，乱成了一锅粥。

这锅粥里，却没有他爹的声音。

小满手脚并用，一口气往上爬，爬得比方才快了一倍，左手腕疼得眼前一阵一阵发黑，也顾不得了。爬到崖腰，头顶上垂下来一根麻绳，他没去抓那根绳子，因为绳子旁边，还伸下来一只手。

那只手五根指头张着，指甲缝里全是泥，手背上划了好几道口子，血和泥糊在一起，已经干了。它往下伸着，伸得太长了，长得不像一只人的手。小满认得这只手。昨儿在这道坡上，它擦过他的手腕，没抓住。

他伸出右手，抓住了它。

这一回，它抓住了。

那只手一使劲，小满整个人便给拽了上去，拽得两只脚在崖壁上乱蹬，蹬下来好几块泥。他还没站稳，已给一把搂进了一个怀里，搂得喘不过气来。那怀里一股泥腥味，一股汗酸味，还有一股烟袋锅子的味道——是老周的烟袋，他爹不抽烟，在这坡上待了一夜，大约是给老周的烟味熏上的。他爹整个人都在抖，抖得比肩上那只狐狸还厉害，抖得小满的牙齿都跟着打颤。

他爹趴在崖边一夜，膝盖上缠的麻布全是泥，脸上也全是泥，一双眼睛通红，红得跟兔子一般。他就那么搂着儿子，嘴张着，一个字都没喊出来。方才喊了一夜，大约是把一辈子的字，全都喊完了。

小满说道：「爹，我没事。你的膝盖——」

他爹只道：「闭嘴。」

这是小满这辈子，第一次听他爹凶他。

这几个人是天没亮便上山的。原来前一日天黑透了，还不见爷儿俩回来，小满他娘便摸黑敲开了老周家的门。老周点了火把，一直走到断碑底下，却不敢过去——过了断碑，树会自己挪地方，路会自己打结，这话是村里的老人说了几十年的，夜里谁也不敢拿自己去试。他在碑底下蹲到天蒙蒙亮，才叫上两个后生，扛着绳子、门板，认着树上的记号一道一道寻进来。小满刻的那四十一道记号，原是给他爹认路的，没想到头一个认着它走进黑松岭的，是老周。至于他爹，哪里也没去，就在这道坡上，趴了一整夜，冲着底下喊了一整夜。老周说到这里，拿烟袋锅子在鞋底上磕了磕，瞧了他爹一眼，道：「你爹，犟。」他爹没吭声。小满知道老周说的不对。他爹不是犟，他爹是这辈子头一回，没听别人的。
story.en:
He turned his face a little toward the fur on his shoulder and cleared his throat. There were things, he thought, that ought to be said now. Last night he'd talked to it all night — about his mother, his father's knee, Ahe's eggs, the bowl, everything under the sun — and left out just this one. It had opened the vine wall for him and coughed blood; last night it had nearly stopped breathing — all of that had to be said properly. So he said, very formally: "Yinyue."

"Mm."

"Last night… no, this morning… no, that's not right either." He thought, and decided not to bother about when. "Anyway, I want to say to you —"

"Your father's calling you, up there."

Xiaoman stopped.

"All night," its voice was very low. "His voice is gone; you can't hear it. This king can. …Answer him first."

Xiaoman pricked his ears upward. The wind came moaning down from the clifftop, and in the wind, sure enough, there was a voice, so hoarse it hardly sounded human, calling over and over — calling his name. It called once, rested, called again, very slowly, as if every call had to be dug out of the throat bit by bit.

He opened his mouth to answer and only then found his own voice was gone too — talked hoarse all night to a fox. He drew a full breath and bellowed: "Da-a-ad —!" It came out cracked and shrill, not much better than a duck with its tail trodden on. Above, the calling broke off at once.

Then everything up there went into an uproar. First a gruff voice: "— Here! The mud on the slope's given way! Somebody down there!" — Ahe's father, Old Zhou. Then a babble of voices, footsteps, someone shouting "Rope! Rope!" and someone shouting "Easy, don't all crowd the edge, it's still sliding," a proper pot of porridge.

In that porridge there was no voice of his father's.

Xiaoman scrambled up on hands and feet, climbing twice as fast as before, his left wrist aching till his sight went black in waves; he didn't care. At the halfway ledge a hemp rope dropped down beside him. He didn't take the rope, because beside the rope a hand was reaching down too.

Five fingers spread, mud under every nail, several cuts across the back of it, blood and mud caked dry together. It reached down, reached too far, too long to look like a human hand. Xiaoman knew this hand. Yesterday, on this slope, it had brushed his wrist and not caught hold.

He reached out his right hand and took it.

This time, it caught.

The hand heaved, and Xiaoman was hauled up, feet scrabbling on the rock and kicking down clods of mud. Before he'd found his footing he was crushed into an embrace so tight he couldn't breathe. It smelled of mud and sour sweat and pipe smoke — Old Zhou's pipe; his father didn't smoke; a night on this slope beside Old Zhou had smoked him through. His father was shaking all over, shaking harder than the fox on his shoulder, shaking so that Xiaoman's teeth chattered with it.

His father had lain at the cliff edge all night; the hemp round his knee was all mud, his face all mud, his eyes red as a rabbit's. He just held his son, mouth open, and not a word came out. He'd called all night; he'd probably called out every word he had in his life.

Xiaoman said, "Dad, I'm all right. Your knee —"

His father said only: "Shut up."

It was the first time in his life Xiaoman had heard his father be harsh with him.

The men had come up before dawn. The evening before, when full dark fell and father and son still weren't back, Xiaoman's mother had felt her way through the dark and knocked on Old Zhou's door. Old Zhou lit a torch and went as far as the broken stele — but didn't dare go past; past the stele the trees move of themselves and the paths tie themselves in knots, as the old folk had said for decades, and nobody would test that on himself at night. He crouched under the stele till the sky paled, then fetched two young men, and with rope and a door-plank they followed the marks on the trees, one by one. The forty-one marks Xiaoman cut had been meant to guide his father; who'd have thought the first to walk into Black Pine Ridge by them would be Old Zhou. As for his father, he'd gone nowhere at all — he'd lain on that slope the whole night, calling down the whole night. Here Old Zhou knocked his pipe on his sole and glanced at the father. "Your dad. Stubborn." His father said nothing. Xiaoman knew Old Zhou had it wrong. His father wasn't stubborn; for the first time in his life, his father hadn't done as someone else said.
